title: Safeguard low-latency flows from long-request dominance in continuous-batching scheduler
creator: Aisha Raman
description: Summary: Multiple customers (hosted and Dedicated customers, plus one private deployment) reported recurring high tail latency for small requests during traffic bursts where a minority of very long-context requests saturated the batching pipeline. Investigation revealed the scheduler orders and merge heuristics are using request-count and arrival-time only, which allowed large-token requests to dominate batch formation and cause starvation of latency-sensitive flows. This ticket tracks a production-safe fix (scoped and rollable) that re-weights scheduling heuristics by estimated token footprint and implements a fast-path preemptive flush for low-token requests. The fix addresses Hosted, Dedicated, and Private variants and includes telemetry, compatibility flags, canary rollout, and customer communications.
acceptance_criteria: Scheduler orders by estimated token footprint and SLA weight; e2e bench shows <=10% regression on throughput for long-context workloads
P95 tail for small (<128 tokens) requests returns to baseline under burst tests on Hosted and Dedicated clusters
Feature flag exists to disable new ordering logic for Private customers; configuration documented
Automated canary shows no increased error rates or memory regressions after 48h
Customer incidents for this pattern remain resolved for two rolling weeks after rollout
steps: Add estimated_tokens field to incoming request envelope (best-effort heuristic from content-length + model token-ratio)
Change merge comparator to compute score = SLA_weight * (1 / (1 + estimated_tokens)) + age_boost; prefer lower estimated_tokens for latency buckets
Introduce a small_request_fastpath: if request estimated_tokens <= 128 and queue_time > 20ms then preemptively flush batch (configurable)
Add backpressure guard to avoid oscillation: maintain moving average of tokens-per-second and apply soft caps to prevent long-request flood from trimming small-request servicing below threshold
Expose three knobs in runtime config for Hosted/Dedicated: token_weight, fastpath_threshold, backpressure_alpha
Add instrumentation: per-route tokens_queued, preemptive_flush_count, starved_request_count, and batch_size_token_histogram
Unit and integration tests for comparator, plus stress tests with mixed small/large request mixes
Staging canary with synthetic traffic; compare p50/p95/p99 small-request latencies; run smoke on Dedicated pool
Canary rollout to 5% of Hosted capacity for 24h, widen to 25% for 48h, then full rollout; Dedicated to be coordinated with customers and ops
Private release notes and a patch bundle; offer assisted upgrade for customers with custom kernels

testing_plan: Unit tests for comparator with edge cases (zero tokens, extremely large estimates)
Integration stress test harness with mixed traffic ratios (50/50, 80/20, 95/5 small/large)
Chaos test: inject synthetic long-request flood while verifying small-request latencies remain under alert threshold
Memory and KV cache integration test to ensure preemptive flush doesn't cause cache eviction storms
Dedicated customer smoke test with their sample workload prior to rollout
risks_and_mitigations: Risk: Estimation heuristic mispredicts token count for some encodings -> Mitigation: fall back to request-length-based conservative upper bound and expose knob to tune ratio
Risk: Fastpath preemptive flush could increase total latency for long jobs -> Mitigation: config alpha and gradual rollout; track overall tokens-per-second to ensure throughput targets
Risk: Oscillation between fastpath and backpressure -> Mitigation: add moving-average damping term and a minimum dwell time between mode switches
Risk: Private deployments on older runtimes cannot accept runtime flag -> Mitigation: provide patch bundle and runtime migration checklist
